title: Observation of g-wave altermagnetic multipole
authors: Ryo Misawa, Rikuto Oiwa, Shunsuke Kitou, Tatsuya Miki, Motohiko Ezawa, Weiyi Yun, Rinsuke Yamada, Chihaya Koyama, J. Alberto Rodríguez Velamazán, Kamil K. Kolincio, Navid Qureshi, Elina Zhakina, Yuiga Nakamura, Jan Masell, Ilya Belopolski, Taka-hisa Arima, Yusuke Nomura, Satoru Hayami, Max Hirschberger
abstract: Over the past few years, altermagnets have emerged as a new class of collinear magnets with broken time-reversal symmetry, offering novel opportunities for spintronics beyond conventional magnets. Rather than from net magnetization, as in ferromagnets, the unconventional time-reversal symmetry breaking of altermagnets originates from antiferroic magnetic dipoles locked to higher-order multipoles. Here we report the direct visualization of a $g$-wave altermagnetic multipole in the canonical altermagnet CrSb. Combining high-energy synchrotron X-ray diffraction with valence electron density (VED) analysis, we uncover a pronounced directional anisotropy of the VED distribution alternating between Cr sublattices. This evidences the antiferroic order of electric hexadecapoles predicted in $g$-wave altermagnets. Its coexistence with antiferroic magnetic dipoles induces ferroic magnetic multipoles, as probed by polarized neutron diffraction. We further identify a microscopic model of altermagnetism that directly relates the $g$-wave multipole and the $g$-wave spin splitting. Through direct observation and quantification of multipoles, this study provides a real-space fingerprint of altermagnetism and establishes a general probe of hidden multipole order in quantum materials.
summary: This paper reports the direct experimental observation of a $g$-wave electric multipole in the altermagnet CrSb using synchrotron X-ray diffraction. By analyzing the directional anisotropy of the Valence Electron Density, the authors confirm the existence of this higher-order multipole, establishing a real-space fingerprint of altermagnetism. This work connects subtle electric multipole order to measurable magnetic phenomena, advancing the field of quantum materials.
main_problem: To directly visualize and establish a real-space fingerprint of altermagnetism, specifically the hidden multipole order, in a material like CrSb.
main_result: The study successfully observed a pronounced, alternating directional anisotropy in the Valence Electron Density (VED) around Cr sites, confirming the presence of the predicted $g$-wave electric multipole order.
method: The research combines high-energy synchrotron X-ray diffraction with Valence Electron Density (VED) analysis, complemented by theoretical modeling using symmetry-adapted Wannier functions and polarized neutron diffraction measurements.
model_or_system: The physical system is the altermagnet CrSb. The theoretical framework models the electronic structure using a tight-binding Hamiltonian expanded in terms of electric multipoles ($\hat{Q}_{lm}$), relating the $g$-wave multipole to the spin splitting.
key_observables: Valence Electron Density (VED) anisotropy, the $g$-wave multipole term ($\alpha$), and the magnetic flipping ratio (FR) from polarized neutron diffraction.
important_parameters: The $g$-wave multipole amplitude ($	ext{Q}_{43}$), which was quantified to $0.21(6)$.
main_assumptions: The VED is approximated as a linear combination of electric multipoles, and the spin splitting is modeled as being proportional to the $g$-wave multipole amplitude.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the predicted antiferroic pattern of electric hexadecapoles, the crystal structure of CrSb, and the experimentally observed VED anisotropy around the Cr sublattices.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the theoretical necessity of higher-order multipoles in altermagnets, to presenting the experimental VED measurements confirming the $g$-wave multipole, and finally linking this electric order to measurable magnetic properties like spin splitting via polarized neutron diffraction.
why_interesting: The work provides a concrete, measurable link between higher-order electric multipole moments (like the $g$-wave hexadecapole) and observable electronic/magnetic properties, which is crucial for understanding exotic magnetic states beyond simple dipole moments.
